newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, SPD to hold "last chance" German tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, SPD to hold "last chance" German tax talks.

text.p: Germany's ruling parties and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) met separately on Monday to fine-tune their positions ahead of tax talks described as a last chance to win the battle against soaring unemployment.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl will meet SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine at 1400 GMT to seek a compromise on a coalition plan to cut 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in taxes to boost job-creation after Germany's January unemployment hit 4.7 million -- the highest since 1933.
Failure to reach agreement would mean tax legislation would face a tortuous path through parliament, where parts could be blocked by the SPD through its majority in the upper house.
Kohl, speaking ahead of a meeting of his Christian Democrats (CDU) said: "Both sides must now put their cards on the table."
Leaders of Kohl's 14-year-old coalition appealed to the SPD to show willingness to compromise.
"Today is a decisive day for conquering unemployment," Peter Hintze, CDU general secretary told ZDF public television.

Hintze called on the SPD to be ready to hold a constructive dialogue. "If both sides enter the talks without preconditions and are ready to work fairly on reforms, the talks could lead to success," he told ZDF.
Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), called the meeting "one of the last big chances for politicians to win the battle against unemployment."
Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax proposals foresee big cuts in income and corporate tax rates over the next two years, offset in part by abolishing over 70 tax breaks.

The SPD has said it was willing to compromise on some measures, but opposes Waigel's plan to cut the top income tax rate to 39 percent from 53 percent. It hardened its rhetoric ahead of the summit, saying the tax reforms must benefit normal wage earners by cutting non-wage costs.

"We are obliged to help the nation, not the government," SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told ZDF. He said he wanted to "create order, reduce the burdens on citizens, to revive the economy -- but not to perfume a pile of manure."
He said his party would not make concessions on tax breaks for those who work unsocial hours, the elimination of which is a key part of Waigel's reform plan.

The unusual meeting between Kohl and Lafontaine is seen as a round of high-stakes poker ahead of 1998 elections and the start of European monetary union (EMU) in 1999. Unemployment and failing tax revenues are jeopardising Bonn's bid to reduce its budget deficit this year below the ceiling of three percent of GDP specified in EMU's guiding Maastricht treaty.
In a separate radio interview, Scharping said Waigel's plans would tear a 50 billion mark hole in the budget.
"In a nation with 4.7 million unemployed, we cannot afford to waste time or be unclear about the issues," he said.
Monday's talks are unlikely to bring quick results, but if they start well, they could set in motion a deal-making process which would circumvent lengthy parliamentary wrangling.
Analysts at Deutsche Bank Research said in a research note on Monday a compromise was in sight and signs were increasing that key parts of the reform could be brought forward to 1998.
"It would be better to bring the whole reform forward to 1998. That could, however, endanger the credibility of the process of consolidating public finances," Deutsche Bank said.
It added: "The less the whole tax reform is watered down and the quicker it is cleared up, the sooner we can expect impulses for the economy."
($ = 1.676 German Marks)
